newsitem.title: BELGIUM: E.U. probes firms breaking anti-boycott laws.
newsitem.headline: E.U. probes firms breaking anti-boycott laws.

text.p: Dozens of European companies are being investigated on suspicion they are breaking European Union laws and undermining its efforts to counter a U.S. law designed to punish companies for doing certain types of business in Cuba, according to trade sources.
"They are keeping it quiet, but the European Commission is looking into the activities of dozens of companies to see if they have broken the law," one trade analyst told Reuters.
The EU passed laws in October as a foil to part of the Helms-Burton Act, the culmination of years of U.S. policy aimed at isolating the Cuban government of Fidel Castro.
"The Commission is very, very disappointed with the lack of support it is getting from European companies in fighting Helms-Burton and has started to take action," he said.
A Commission spokesman told Reuters the EU legislation "was law and had to be followed up."

"The anti-blocking legislation is a powerful response to Helms-Burton," said Peter Guilford, spokesman for Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan. "Inevitably it puts companies in a difficult position. In order to make it effective we have to dig."

Among other things, the U.S. act allows American citizens to sue any foreign company or individual deemed to have gained from investments in former U.S. property confiscated by the Cuban government since the communist revolution of 1959.

Although this section has twice been suspended by President Clinton, the State Department has pressed ahead with compiling a watch list against foreign companies that may be investing in such property.

To counter this threat, the EU passed laws making it illegal for European companies to cooperate with any U.S. investigation and also to prevent firms from pulling out of Cuba on the basis of a U.S. probe.

The laws were designed to present a unified European response to the U.S. act -- which the EU considers extra-territorial -- and also to protect companies that choose not to disinvest their Cuban interests.
Although Washington will not say how many or which companies it has identified, trade analysts say it is "a great deal more" than the three identified last year.

Executives from Italian telecommunications company Ste, Canadian mining conglomorate Sherrit Internationa and Mexican telecommunications firm Grupo Domo were placed on a U.S. blacklist in July and barred from entering the United States because of their links to Cuba.
Under the EU's blocking laws, companies are obliged to tell the commission as soon as they are approached by U.S. authorities.
However, the trade sources said that not a single European company has come forward to say the State Department had contacted them.

"By not coming forward, the commission believes these companies are playing right into the hands of the Americans," a trade expert said. "The commission believes this undermines its action in trying to overturn the act."
